corrected_draft.title: HHS Removes 17 Members From CDC Vaccine Advisory Committee

corrected_draft.description_medium: On June 9, 2025, HHS announced it had removed all 17 sitting members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and would replace them with new members then under consideration. The committee advises CDC on vaccine safety, efficacy, and clinical need. The HHS announcement supports a discrete membership action but contradicts the held entry’s February 10 date.
corrected_draft.description_long: On June 9, 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services announced that it had removed the 17 sitting members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and would replace them with new members then under consideration. ACIP advises the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on vaccine safety, efficacy, and clinical need. HHS said the action was taken under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and described it as a total reconstitution of the committee. HHS also said ACIP would next meet June 25 through 27 at CDC headquarters in Atlanta. The announcement establishes the date and scope of the membership change. It does not support the held entry’s February 10 date; that date should be removed. The corrected record should attribute HHS’s stated rationale to the department and distinguish it from independent assessment of the committee’s scientific role or the effects of the membership change.

corrected_draft.title: 2025 Law Narrows SNAP Eligibility for Many Lawfully Present Immigrants
corrected_draft.description_short: The 2025 law restricted SNAP eligibility for many lawfully present immigrants, while retaining exceptions.
corrected_draft.description_medium: The 2025 reconciliation law, signed July 4, amended SNAP eligibility rules for noncitizens. NILC’s review says many previously eligible lawfully present groups—including refugees, asylees, some trafficking survivors, and certain parolees—were excluded unless they adjust to another qualifying status. Exceptions remain, and households may retain benefits for eligible members. The held title overstates the change as affecting all legal immigrants.
corrected_draft.description_long: President Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, P.L. 119-21, on July 4, 2025. Section 10108 changed SNAP eligibility for noncitizens. The National Immigration Law Center’s review of the statute and USDA implementation materials says the new rule narrows eligibility for many immigrants who previously qualified, including refugees, asylees, people granted withholding of removal, some survivors of trafficking or domestic violence, certain special immigrant visa holders, parolees, and other specified groups. The law retains eligibility for lawful permanent residents, certain Cuban and Haitian immigrants, and people covered by the Compact of Free Association, with other exceptions under prior law. NILC says new applicants are subject to the restrictions immediately under USDA guidance, while households already receiving SNAP are affected at recertification; it also notes confusion in the implementation guidance. Because SNAP eligibility is household-based, eligible U.S.-citizen family members may continue receiving benefits even when another member becomes ineligible. The original wording that the law eliminated benefits for all legal immigrants is too broad.

corrected_draft.title: New York Appeals Court Modifies Trump Organization Fraud Judgment
corrected_draft.description_short: A divided New York appeals court vacated disgorgement awards in the Trump civil-fraud case but otherwise affirmed parts of the judgment.
corrected_draft.description_medium: The New York Appellate Division’s Aug. 21, 2025 opinion describes trial findings that Trump and Trump Organization entities submitted deceptive financial statements to lenders and others to obtain business benefits, including favorable loan terms. The divided appellate disposition vacated disgorgement awards and otherwise affirmed portions of the judgment. This is a dated court event; it should not be described as loans made to Trump personally at favorable rates.
corrected_draft.description_long: On August 21, 2025, the Appellate Division of New York’s First Department issued its decision in People v. Trump, an appeal from the civil-fraud judgment concerning statements of financial condition prepared by Donald Trump and Trump Organization executives. The court’s opinion describes the trial court’s finding that defendants repeatedly submitted deceptive business records to lenders, insurers, and other counterparties to obtain financial benefits. The appellate disposition was divided: it modified the judgment to vacate disgorgement awards and otherwise affirmed, while separate opinions disagreed about aspects of the analysis and remedy. The ruling concerns financial statements and business loans involving Trump Organization entities, with Trump’s personal guarantees relevant to some transactions. It does not support the held record’s simplified claim that the organization made loans to Trump himself at favorable rates, nor should it be characterized as an unqualified final determination of every alleged tax-manipulation claim. The corrected record should focus on the dated appellate ruling and describe the modified disposition.
